title: Granny square rectangle shawl
subtitle: A 5 x 20 grid of 10 cm granny squares in 3+ DK colours, joined flat into a 100 cm x 200 cm shawl
excerpt: One hundred 10 cm granny squares worked in three or more DK colours and joined flat into a 5 x 20 grid. The finished rectangle measures 100 cm wide by 200 cm long and is worn as a wrap or a large scarf. Joining is done flat using a join-as-you-go method on the final round of each square so the seams form a decorative ridge on the right side.
sourceNotes: Granny square construction from Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 1 (1886), which describes a four-corner square worked from the centre out in rounds. Flat join-as-you-go joining method synthesised from documented fibre arts technique; no single prior source.
heroPrompt: A rectangular granny-square wrap in deep jewel tones -- burgundy, forest green, mustard, and navy DK -- laid flat on a pale wooden floor, the 5 x 20 grid clearly visible.

crochet.gaugeText: Each granny square measures 10 x 10 cm after blocking with DK yarn on a 4 mm hook.
crochet.finishedSizeText: Approximately 100 cm wide x 200 cm long (5 squares x 20 squares), after blocking.

glossaryTerms.definition: A square crochet motif worked from the centre out in rounds. Each round works groups of trebles separated by chain spaces; the corners are formed by a longer chain space.

A flat joining method where the final round of each new square is modified: instead of closing the corner and side chain spaces freely, you draw a chain loop through the corresponding space on the adjacent already-completed square. The join is visible as a neat ridge on the right side.

content.text: This rectangle shawl is built from 100
granny squares

arranged in a 5-wide by 20-long grid. Each square is worked in three rounds from the centre out on a 4 mm hook, with a colour change between rounds or between squares. The squares are connected during the final joining round of each new square using the
join-as-you-go
method, so no sewing is needed after the squares are complete.

The pattern uses at least three colours but works with any number. A planned colour layout (drawn out on a grid before you begin) avoids the same colour appearing in adjacent squares. The final round of every square is worked in the same joining colour to give the grid a consistent visual frame.

attrs.title: Materials
attrs.body: Approximately 500 g total DK-weight yarn across 3 or more colours. A 4 mm hook (US G/6). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Stitch markers. Blocking mat and pins. Tape measure. Pen and grid paper for a colour plan (optional but helpful with 100 squares).

content.text: Gauge

Each granny square measures 10 x 10 cm after blocking with DK yarn on a 4 mm hook. Work one square, block it by dampening and pinning to a 10 x 10 cm square, and measure before working all 100. If your square is larger than 10 cm, drop a hook size; if smaller, go up a hook size. The correct square size is what controls the finished shawl dimensions.
Stitches used
ch: chain -- UK and US shared.
sl st: slip stitch -- UK and US shared.
dc: double crochet (UK) -- used in the joining round edging.
tr: treble (UK) -- the main stitch of the granny square body. The same move as US double crochet (dc).
Pattern
Individual granny square (first square only)
Using colour A, ch 4. Sl st in 1st ch to form a ring.
Round 1: Ch 3 (counts as 1 tr). 2 tr in ring. Ch 2. *3 tr in ring. Ch 2.* Repeat from * to * twice more. Sl st in top of starting ch-3 to close. Fasten off. (4 corner spaces, 12 tr)

Round 2: Join colour B in any corner ch-2 space. Ch 3 (counts as 1 tr). 2 tr in same corner space. Ch 2. 3 tr in same corner space. *Ch 1. 3 tr in next corner space. Ch 2. 3 tr in same corner space.* Repeat from * to * twice more. Ch 1. Sl st in top of starting ch-3 to close. Fasten off. (4 corners each with 2 groups of 3 tr, 4 side spaces)

Round 3 (joining round): Join joining colour in any corner ch-2 space. Ch 3 (counts as 1 tr). 2 tr in same corner space. Ch 2. 3 tr in same corner space. *Ch 1. 3 tr in next side ch-1 space. Ch 1. 3 tr in corner ch-2 space. Ch 2. 3 tr in same corner space.* Repeat from * to * twice more. Ch 1. 3 tr in remaining side ch-1 space. Ch 1. Sl st in top of starting ch-3. Fasten off. (4 corners, 8 side groups, 24 tr)
Join-as-you-go: joining to an existing square

On all squares except the first, modify round 3 along any shared edge. Where the pattern says "ch 2" at a corner shared with an adjacent square: instead of ch 2, work ch 1, then insert hook into the matching corner ch-2 space on the adjacent square and draw up a loop, sl st to join, then ch 1. Where the pattern says "ch 1" at a side space shared with an adjacent square: instead of ch 1, insert hook into the matching ch-1 space on the adjacent square and sl st. Continue in pattern for all other spaces. This produces a flat join visible as a chain ridge on the right side.
Assembly order

Work the grid in columns from left to right, building each column from bottom to top. Square 1 is the bottom-left corner. Squares 2 to 5 complete the first column. Square 6 joins to the right side of square 1 and to no other square. Continue column by column. Squares joining in the middle of the grid will join to one square below and one square to the left simultaneously: work the ch-1 and ch-2 modifications on both the bottom and left edges of round 3 at the same time. (100 squares total)
Finishing

Weave in all ends through the backs of stitches on the wrong side. Because each square is small and each colour change is short, there are many ends; allow time for this step. Wet-block the completed rectangle by soaking in cool water, pressing out excess water in a towel, then pinning to the stated dimensions on a blocking mat.
Care

Handwash in cool water with mild detergent. Do not tumble-dry. Lay flat and ease to shape while damp. If colours are deep or mixed-fibre, test for colourfastness by wetting a small corner and pressing against a white cloth before the first full wash.
What to try next

A 6 x 6 grid of the same square makes a cushion cover front. Adding a fourth round to every square before joining produces a coarser, heavier blanket throw from the same grid proportions. Mixing square sizes (some worked to round 2 only) creates a playful patchwork surface where smaller and larger squares fill the same column width.
